scope: All 212 current resources plus all 66 resource candidate leads. Source-supported short descriptions checked; this is not a full-paper or full-video read claim.

lead_dispositions.name: awesome-vla-wam
lead_dispositions.evidence: Current README places RL papers within its VLA list rather than in a dedicated RL section; its top-level categories support the revised list description.

proposed_fields.one_line: Curated VLA and world-action-model research list with latent action models, human action pretraining, robotic agentics, surveys, datasets, benchmarks and hardware; RL papers appear within the VLA list.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The one_line says the list includes 'RL-for-VLA sections'. The current README has no such section. RL-for-VLA papers (SimpleVLA-RL, VLA-RL, RIPT-VLA) appear only as ordinary bullets inside the flat 'VLA Models' list. The line also leaves out sections the list does have: Robotic Agentics, Policies, Physics Engine, Software and Hardware.

lead_dispositions.name: Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies
lead_dispositions.evidence: Abstract and introduction: 2,331 real evaluations over three tasks; typically 20–40% fewer evaluation trials than random testing. Expressed as trials saved rather than an undefined efficiency percentage.

proposed_fields.one_line: Sequential experimental design uses a probabilistic surrogate over task factors for real-robot evaluation. Across 2,331 trials on three tasks, the authors report typically needing at least 20-40% fewer trials than random testing.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: 'roughly 20-40% more efficient than random testing' restates the paper's claim in different units and drops its 'at least'. The paper says the method typically needs at least 20-40% fewer trials, which it explains as saving 20-40 trials out of a 100-trial budget. That is a cut in trial count, not 'X% more efficient'. The line also omits the scale (2,331 real-world evaluations). Optionally, the org can be filled in: arXiv HTML lists all four authors at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities.

lead_dispositions.name: BEHAVIOR-1K: A Human-Centered, Embodied AI Benchmark with 1,000 Everyday Activities and Realistic Simulation
lead_dispositions.evidence: Abstract specifies 1,000 everyday activities in 50 scenes including gardens, restaurants and offices, with 9,000+ objects. Household-only wording was too narrow.

proposed_fields.one_line: Simulation benchmark of 1,000 long-horizon everyday activities across 50 scenes (homes, gardens, restaurants, offices) and 9,000+ annotated objects, built on OmniGibson with rigid, deformable and liquid physics.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The line calls the 1,000 activities 'household'. The paper calls them 'everyday activities', and its 50 scenes include gardens, restaurants and offices as well as houses. This is a small inaccuracy; the other numbers (1,000 activities, 50 scenes, 9,000+ objects, OmniGibson with rigid/deformable/liquid physics) are correct.

lead_dispositions.name: awesome-physical-ai
lead_dispositions.evidence: Current raw README has a placeholder arXiv identifier for CO-RFT. Used existing VLA-RL, FLaRe and SimpleVLA-RL examples instead.

proposed_fields.one_line: Curated paper list on Physical AI: VLAs, world models, action representations, and learning paradigms including a section on RL for VLA policies (e.g. VLA-RL, FLaRe, SimpleVLA-RL).

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Low severity. CO-RFT is one of the three examples the one_line names. In the linked list, the CO-RFT entry points to a placeholder link (arxiv.org/abs/2601.XXXXX) and is dated 'arXiv, 2026'. Several neighbouring entries also have placeholder links (HICRA 2601.XXXXX, RL4VLA 2409.XXXXX, TPO and ReinboT 2505.XXXXX). Using a broken entry as a headline example invites criticism. The section's own description, 'RL-based methods for optimizing VLA policies', is accurate. Swapping in an example with a working link fixes it.

lead_dispositions.name: Critical Interval MSE: Toward Reliable Offline Validation for Robot Manipulation Policies
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper distinguishes 27 simulated checkpoints with Spearman −0.87 versus −0.61 from four real-robot tasks supporting the same trend. Correlation setting is now explicit.

proposed_fields.one_line: Offline validation metric computing action MSE only on task-critical segments, with action alignment; across 27 simulated checkpoints, Spearman -0.87 with rollout success vs -0.61 for raw MSE; real-robot tests on four tasks agree.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The entry mixes up sim and real. It says Spearman -0.87 is 'with real rollout success', but the paper gets -0.87 vs -0.61 across 27 simulated checkpoints (X-VLA-based variants, Table 1 'Simulation model variants'). The real-robot experiments are separate: four tasks, scored by Elo, and the paper calls them 'consistent with' the simulation results.

lead_dispositions.name: LIBERO-Plus: In-depth Robustness Analysis of Vision-Language-Action Models
lead_dispositions.evidence: Already resolved before this review: placeholder affiliation replaced with source-listed institutions.
lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The org field holds a leftover placeholder, 'Not confirmed on fetched pages', which would show up publicly in README/site. The paper does list its affiliations. The one_line checks out: 10,030 tasks, 7 factors, 95% to below 30%, language ignored.

lead_dispositions.name: CaP-X: A Framework for Benchmarking and Improving Coding Agents for Robot Manipulation
lead_dispositions.evidence: Abstract qualifies near-human reliability as achieved on several tasks. Retained the CaP-Gym/CaP-Bench, multi-turn interaction and sim-to-real components without universalizing that result.

proposed_fields.one_line: Code-as-policy framework: CaP-Gym, CaP-Bench (12 frontier models), training-free CaP-Agent0 using multi-turn interaction and visual differencing to reach near human-level reliability on several tasks, plus CaP-RL with sim2real transfer.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Overclaim. The entry says CaP-Agent0 achieves 'human-level reliability' with no qualifier. The paper says this only for several manipulation tasks: the API abstract says 'recovers human-level reliability on several manipulation tasks' and the v2 HTML abstract says 'near human-level'. The '12 models', visual differencing and CaP-RL sim-to-real parts are correct.

lead_dispositions.name: FailBench: How Reliable are VLMs at Judging Robot Task Success?
lead_dispositions.evidence: Reported benchmark totals: 2,197 attempts, 14 sources, 13 detectors; best mean balanced accuracy 0.77. Contact-rich assembly maximum is exactly 0.60, so below-0.60 wording was inaccurate.

proposed_fields.one_line: Benchmark of 2,197 manipulation attempts from 14 sources (12 real, 2 sim) for VLM success detection; best of 13 detectors reaches 0.77 mean balanced accuracy, and no model exceeds 0.60 on contact-rich assembly.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: As worded, the one_line credits the best model with 'under 0.60 on contact-heavy assembly'. The paper body says no model exceeds 0.60 there, and the best detector (Gemini 3 Flash) scores exactly 0.60 on that subset (reassemble), so 'under 0.60' is wrong for the best model. Also, 0.77 is the mean (macro) balanced accuracy of the best of 13 detectors.

lead_dispositions.name: From Rollout to Reset: A Graph-Based Harness for Autonomous Long-Horizon Manipulation Evaluation (HALTER)
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper reports scene restoration 76% versus AutoEval 52% and operator-time reduction 72% versus manual reset on four Franka tasks. Baselines and metric now identified.

proposed_fields.one_line: LLM over point-cloud scene graphs scores rollouts, plans resets from atomic reset skills and verifies them; on four long-horizon Franka tasks, 76% scene restoration vs 52% AutoEval, and 72% less operator time than manual reset.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: '72% less operator time' has no baseline. The paper measures it against manual reset. The setting (four long-horizon tasks on a Franka arm) is also missing. The 76% vs 52% AutoEval figure is correct.

lead_dispositions.name: Faster and Better? Benchmark Bugs and Design Limitations Distort the Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Acceleration
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper reports 22 bugs and four design limitations across seven simulated benchmarks. Baseline ranking reversal from last to first is a particular LIBERO-PRO task example.

proposed_fields.one_line: Audits seven simulated VLA benchmarks (RoboTwin, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench...), finding 22 bugs and 4 design limitations; fixes can reverse acceleration-method rankings, moving the baseline from last to first on one LIBERO-PRO task.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: 'Sometimes moving the baseline from last to first' suggests this happened more than once. The paper reports it on one task, LIBERO-PRO Spatial-Task. The other counts (seven benchmarks, 22 bugs, 4 design limitations) are correct.

lead_dispositions.name: BiGym: A Demo-Driven Mobile Bi-Manual Manipulation Benchmark
lead_dispositions.evidence: BiGym paper author block identifies Dyson Robot Learning Lab. Repository hosting by Neuracore does not establish the original paper affiliation.
lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The org attribution is off. The repo is now hosted under the NeuracoreAI GitHub org, but the paper lists one affiliation for all authors: Dyson Robot Learning Lab. Writing 'Neuracore' credits the work to the wrong institution. The URL resolves and is the official repo (the README points to it). The one_line is correct: MuJoCo, 40 tasks, human demos, proprioception plus RGB/depth from 3 cameras, IL and demo-driven RL baselines.

lead_dispositions.name: EmbodiedSWE: Coding Agents for Long Horizon Dexterous Robotics
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper author block includes ByteDance Seed alongside Princeton, Yale, CMU and Stanford; retained a non-exhaustive affiliation list.

proposed_fields.org: Princeton, Yale, ByteDance Seed, CMU, Stanford et al.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Minor. The org list is accurate but incomplete. It leaves out ByteDance Seed, which is listed first in the paper's affiliations, plus UCLA and UW. Leaving out the first-listed industry affiliation could read as unfair attribution. Adding it with 'et al.' is the smallest fix. The one_line is supported ('up to half an hour of continuous interaction'; a VLA trained only on generated sim demos completes a long-horizon task on a real robot).

lead_dispositions.name: EBRL: Asynchronous Embodied RL by Multi-Grained Resource Management
lead_dispositions.evidence: Abstract and section 6: four simulation benchmarks; throughput 1.30–3.47x; LIBERO-Object/GR00T PPO completes 60 epochs about 2.5x faster than Sync. No public code URL appears in the paper; category retained.

proposed_fields.one_line: Asynchronous RLinf-based scheduler overlaps rollout and training with CPU/GPU resource allocation. Simulation: 1.30-3.47x rollout throughput over prior systems; LIBERO-Object/GR00T PPO completes 60 epochs ~2.5x faster than a synchronous baseline.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The 2.5x convergence number is presented as 'versus prior systems'. In the paper body it is a single setting (LIBERO-Object, GR00T, PPO): wall-clock time to 60 epochs compared with a synchronous ('Sync') baseline. The one_line also does not say the results are simulation-only. A secondary issue: the paper has no code link or open-source statement, so the 'Code: general RL and black-box optimization' section (code-rl) is a weak fit. As an embodied/VLA RL training system it fits code-robot better, but it still has no public code.

lead_dispositions.name: PureJaxRL
lead_dispositions.evidence: README distinguishes about 10x versus single-run CleanRL PyTorch PPO on CartPole/MinAtar from over 1000x against standard PyTorch when many agents run in parallel. Comparison scopes now separate.

proposed_fields.one_line: End-to-end JAX PPO with environment and training compiled together. README reports 10x over single-run CleanRL PyTorch PPO on CartPole/MinAtar-Breakout, and over 1000x over standard PyTorch RL when parallelizing many agents on GPUs.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The speedups leave out their setting, and the 1000x baseline is stated more loosely than in the source. The README gives 10x over CleanRL's PyTorch PPO without vectorization, on CartPole and MinAtar-Breakout. It gives 'over 1000x' against 'standard PyTorch RL implementations' when running many agents in parallel on GPUs. Without the toy environments named, readers may take the numbers as general. The org (Oxford FLAIR) is fine: the author's blog says FLAIR.

lead_dispositions.name: EvoJAX: Hardware-Accelerated Neuroevolution
lead_dispositions.evidence: README compares example runtime on one accelerator (minutes) with CPUs (hours/days). GitHub repository metadata reports archived=true.

proposed_fields.one_line: JAX neuroevolution toolkit running evolution algorithms, policy networks and vectorized tasks in parallel on GPUs/TPUs; README examples run in minutes on a single accelerator versus hours or days on CPUs. Repo now archived.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: 'Experiments finish in minutes instead of hours' drops the baseline and scope. The README says its examples run within minutes on a single accelerator, compared with hours or days on CPUs. The archived status is confirmed (GitHub API archived=true).

lead_dispositions.name: LeanRL
lead_dispositions.evidence: README describes CleanRL-derived single-file scripts, torch.compile and CUDA graphs. GitHub metadata reports archived=true.

proposed_fields.one_line: CleanRL-derived single-file PyTorch RL scripts optimized for speed using torch.compile and CUDA graphs (repo now archived).

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The repo is archived, but the one_line does not say so, unlike the CORL and EvoJAX entries in the same list. The rest of the line is accurate: a CleanRL fork using torch.compile and cudagraphs. The org is fine (meta-pytorch).

lead_dispositions.name: Nevergrad
lead_dispositions.evidence: Rejected: proposed change is stylistic; current short description accurately describes the toolbox.
lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Typo: there is a stray closing parenthesis at the end of the one_line ('optimization).').

lead_dispositions.name: rl_games
lead_dispositions.evidence: README lists PPO, asymmetric actor-critic and SAC with GPU environment support including Isaac Lab and MJLab; replaced a low-information creation date with these supported capabilities.

proposed_fields.one_line: PyTorch RL library with PPO, asymmetric actor-critic and SAC implementations, supporting vectorized GPU environments including Isaac Lab and MJLab.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Not wrong, but uninformative. 'RL implementations library; created January 2019' is trivia (the repo was created 2019-01-13). It leaves out why the library matters for robot policies: PPO/SAC with end-to-end GPU pipelines, and its use in Isaac Gym/Isaac Lab and DeXtreme. This is a low-priority quality fix.

lead_dispositions.name: Robots Need More than VLA and World Models
lead_dispositions.evidence: Author block identifies Motoniq.ai, Stanford, IIT, ETH Zurich, TU Darmstadt and UCL. No Huawei affiliation appears; removed it.

proposed_fields.org: Motoniq.ai; Stanford; IIT; ETH Zurich; TU Darmstadt; UCL

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The org field says one affiliation is Huawei, but the paper does not say that. The paper gives Haitham Bou-Ammar's affiliation as UCL Centre for AI. The field also leaves out Motoniq.ai, which is the affiliation of the first three authors and Mac Schwager's second affiliation.

lead_dispositions.name: A Survey on Reinforcement Learning of Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
lead_dispositions.evidence: Publisher-deposited Crossref abstract retrieved successfully and supports four axes and action/reward/transition design. Author companion README supports the paper-list description. Removed unsupported 100+ count. Full TechRxiv text remains blocked (403), with CDN PDF inaccessible (DNS/502).

proposed_fields.one_line: Survey of RL for VLA manipulation along four axes: RL-VLA architecture (action, reward, transition modeling), online/offline/test-time training paradigms, real-world deployment, and benchmarking; companion Awesome-RL-VLA paper list.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: (a) The org field holds the placeholder 'Not confirmed', which would show up in the published list. No affiliations are visible in the Crossref record, and the TechRxiv page and PDF block automated access (403). (b) The one_line says the survey is organized into offline, online and test-time paradigms. The abstract says the taxonomy has four dimensions, and training paradigms are only one of them. (c) The claim that the companion repo curates '100+ papers' is not supported. The Awesome-RL-VLA README has 89 paper rows in its tables. The other entries are 5 base models, 5 datasets/benchmarks and 2 frameworks, which are not papers. The paper text could not be checked for a 100+ figure.

lead_dispositions.name: Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Policies in Robotics: A Survey and State-Based Locomotion Reproduction
lead_dispositions.evidence: MDPI publisher text was readable in the indexed search result, including abstract and sections 1.3/1.6: 84 studies; five technical axes; five DPPO fine-tuning seeds reuse two BC checkpoints; mean gain 1261.2 return. Gaussian PPO also improves. State-based locomotion only. Direct publisher page/PDF remained 403/429.

proposed_fields.one_line: Scoping review mapping 84 studies with a five-axis taxonomy; in state-based D4RL Hopper, five DPPO fine-tuning seeds gain mean +1261 return over BC initializations. A Gaussian-PPO control also improves, so the gain is not diffusion-specific.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The numbers are correct: 84 studies, a five-axis taxonomy, and a mean +1261.2 return from DPPO over the BC initializations. But the one_line leaves out the paper's own caveat: a Gaussian-policy PPO control also improved, so the gain was not specific to diffusion. It also leaves out that the result covers 5 seeds of state-based locomotion only. Read alone, it suggests the gain comes from diffusion, which the authors explicitly say it does not. The org field is correct.

lead_dispositions.name: Robotic Foundation Models for Industrial Control: A Comprehensive Survey and Readiness Assessment Framework
lead_dispositions.evidence: Survey assesses 324 models over 149 industrial-readiness criteria. The 48,276 decisions are LLM-assisted criterion scores validated by experts, not physical trials.

proposed_fields.one_line: Survey scoring 324 manipulation-capable robot foundation models against 149 industrial-readiness criteria (48,276 LLM-assisted, expert-validated criterion decisions); finds industrial maturity limited and uneven.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: This is a minor clarification. The numbers are exact (324 x 149 = 48,276). But calling them '48,276 evaluations' suggests experts scored each one. The paper says the decisions came from an LLM-assisted pipeline that was checked against expert judgements.

lead_dispositions.name: Workshop on Agentic Robotics (CoRL 2026)
lead_dispositions.evidence: Official workshop page gives November 12 in Austin and submission deadline September 30, 2026 at 11:59 PM AoE. Corrected the prior deadline.

proposed_fields.one_line: CoRL 2026 workshop (Austin, Nov 12) on agents that reason, act and recover on real robots, including self-improvement pipelines and routing corrections to the right abstraction level; submission deadline was September 30, 2026 AoE.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The submission deadline is wrong. The one_line says submissions closed Sep 27, but the workshop page gives Sep 30, 2026. The phrase 'feedback routing' is also vague; the page's own wording is about routing corrections to the abstraction level where they generalize best. The date (Austin, Nov 12), the org list and the scope are correct.

lead_dispositions.name: Sporks of AGI: Why the Real Thing is better than the Next Best Thing
lead_dispositions.evidence: The essay argues real robot data is essential while describing surrogate data as useful supplementation. Reworded as the author’s position and removed unsupported page-level affiliation attribution.

proposed_fields.one_line: Levine essay arguing surrogate data (simulation, human video, hand-held grippers) cannot replace real robot data for broadly generalizing foundation models, and is best used to supplement rather than substitute real-world experience.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: (a) The org 'UC Berkeley; Physical Intelligence' does not appear anywhere in the source. This is Levine's personal Substack and neither the post nor the About page states an affiliation. (b) Tone and fairness: the one_line leaves out the essay's explicit nuance that surrogate data is still useful as a supplement. As written, it reads as a blanket dismissal of sim, human-video and hand-held data, which overstates his position on a public post.

lead_dispositions.name: π*0.6 and RECAP: Teaching Robots to Learn From Their Mistakes
lead_dispositions.evidence: Rejected: the current third-party page explicitly gives 2.1x, 2.3x and 65% to 90%; the lead allegation is unsupported. Numbers remain attributed to this third-party explainer.
lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The explainer does print '2.1x / 2.3x throughput' and 'box assembly 65% -> 90%', but the PI paper's text does not support the exact figures. The paper only says RECAP 'more than doubles' throughput on the hardest tasks and the final box-assembly policy reaches 'about 90%'. The 65% baseline and the 2.1x/2.3x values cannot be found in the primary source (they may come from figures the blog read off), so repeating them risks spreading wrong numbers. Use only claims that both the explainer and the paper support.

lead_dispositions.name: Unfolding Robotics: The Open-Source Recipe for Teaching a Robot to Fold Your Clothes
lead_dispositions.evidence: Official Space MDX reports 131 hours, OpenArm, SARM, reward-weighted BC, DAgger and RTC. Curated-data fine-tuning uses one-fifth the data; experiment 2.5 improves 40% to 90%, evaluated on 20 rollouts (ten per difficulty).

proposed_fields.one_line: OpenArm bimanual pi0/pi0.5 recipe using ~131 h teleoperation, SARM curation, reward-weighted BC, DAgger and real-time chunking. Fine-tuning on a curated dataset one-fifth the size raised shirt-folding success from 40% to 90% across 20 real rollouts.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: '+50 points' is ambiguous, because the article also uses a subtask scoring system measured in 'points' (max 1,500 per experiment). The +50 is percentage points of success rate, from 40% to 90%. The 90% also lacks its denominator: 20 real rollouts, 10 per level, with 100% on Level 1 and 80% on Level 2. Curated high-quality data alone gave only +5 (Exp 2.1). The +50 came from curated data combined with RABC and relative actions, starting from a stronger base, so the wording should follow the article's own summary.

lead_dispositions.name: π0 and π0-FAST: Vision-Language-Action Models for General Robot Control
lead_dispositions.evidence: Hugging Face authored the LeRobot-port explainer. Its fivefold training-speed claim compares pi0-FAST with diffusion-based VLAs, not an unspecified policy; attributed that comparison to the post.

proposed_fields.one_line: Hugging Face post on the LeRobot port of Physical Intelligence's π0 (flow matching, 50Hz actions) and π0-FAST (DCT+BPE action tokens; 5x faster training than diffusion-based VLAs, per the post), with fine-tuning commands.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: '5x faster training' is missing its baseline; the post's claim is 5x faster than diffusion-based VLAs. The org 'Hugging Face; Physical Intelligence' also suggests PI co-authored the post. The bylines are all Hugging Face (Aubakirova, Montalvo, Shukor, Cadene); PI developed the models but did not write the post.

lead_dispositions.name: From Generalists to Specialists: A Case for Real-World RL in Robot Manipulation
lead_dispositions.evidence: USC post describes ReWiND and reports a fivefold improvement after one hour of online interaction; retained attribution rather than interpreting this as a specified absolute success-rate change.

proposed_fields.one_line: USC blog arguing generalist VLAs should specialize via real-world RL; covers ReWiND learned rewards (5x improvement of real-robot policies after 1 hour of online interaction), EXTRACT skill-based RL, and scalable multi-task evaluation.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Minor: '5x in 1 hour' gives no metric or setting. The source means a 5x improvement of robot policies after 1 hour of online interaction, and the ReWiND paper says this is for real-world pretrained bimanual policies. The rest of the line is accurate: authors Jesse Zhang and Abrar Anwar, USC RASC, Sep 24, 2025; covers EXTRACT and probabilistic matrix-completion evaluation.

lead_dispositions.name: Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning (Csaba Szepesvari)
lead_dispositions.evidence: Author’s HTML algorithm list contains 34 entries, 16 boldfaced for accompanying pseudocode. Free PDF availability confirmed; corrected counts.

proposed_fields.one_line: Concise Morgan & Claypool monograph on TD, Monte Carlo, Q-learning, actor-critic, function approximation and exploration; the author's page lists 34 algorithm entries, 16 with pseudocode, and provides a free PDF.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The count '22 with pseudocode' is wrong. The author's page bolds 16 of its 34 listed algorithm entries as having pseudocode. Also, '34 algorithms' is really 34 list entries, because one entry bundles five methods (R-max, MBIE, OI, delayed-Q, MorMax).

lead_dispositions.name: RoboTwin 2.0: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark with Strong Domain Randomization for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper real-world experiment compares synthetic data plus ten real demonstrations against ten real demonstrations alone. The 367% gain is relative. Task/object counts and ICML 2026 attribution match.

proposed_fields.one_line: 50-task bimanual simulator/data generator with five-axis domain randomization (731 objects, 147 categories). In real-world tests, synthetic data plus ten real demos yields a 367% relative VLA gain over the ten-demo baseline; ICML 2026.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The one_line says 'synthetic data gives 367% relative VLA gain' but drops the setting and baseline. The 367% is for a VLA trained on synthetic data PLUS 10 real demos, compared with a baseline trained on only those 10 demos, in real-world tests (42.0% vs 9.0%). Synthetic-only training gives 228%. Everything else checks out: ICML 2026 (repo description), 731 instances / 147 categories, five-axis DR, 50 tasks, and the HKU/SJTU affiliations.

lead_dispositions.name: Robotics benchmarking: where we are, and what comes next
lead_dispositions.evidence: Official benchmarking post assigns 43% single-skill and 4.4% unseen-combination results to fine-tuned GR00T N1.5 on RoboCasa365. They are model results, not benchmark properties.

proposed_fields.one_line: Robot-benchmark survey: fine-tuned GR00T N1.5 averages 43% on RoboCasa365 single-skill tasks versus 4.4% on unseen skill combinations. Argues real-to-sim reconstruction can expose policy weaknesses and guide data collection.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The '43% single skills, 4.4% novel combinations' figures are given without their setting. They are the average success rates of GR00T N1.5 after extra training on 30,000 demos across 300 tasks, evaluated on 50 tasks, as reported in the RoboCasa365 paper the blog cites. Written this way they read like a property of the benchmark itself. Also, 'from YCB to RoboCasa365' understates the scope: the post goes on past RoboCasa365 (VLABench, LIBERO Plus, RoboArena, HumanoidBench, RoboCup@Home and others). Org: the HF byline reads 'projectsim by Kaedim', so 'ProjectSim' is acceptable.

lead_dispositions.name: XPolicyLab: A Unified Standard and Open Ecosystem for Robot Policy Evaluation and Deployment
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper reports 42 policies and O(N+M) integration structure. Five-to-two-hour integration saving comes from one controlled case, not all integrations.

proposed_fields.one_line: Unified observation/action/trajectory schemas and adapters integrate 42 policies, reducing policy-environment integrations from O(NM) to O(N+M). One controlled case reduced integration from over five hours to two; adapters serve RoboTwin, RoboDojo and real robots.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The '5+ hours to 2' figure has lost its setting. It comes from a controlled study of one representative policy, not a general result. The current wording also attaches the speedup to 'across RoboTwin, RoboDojo and real robots', which is really a separate claim (the same adapters serve all three).

lead_dispositions.name: Uncovering and Mitigating Positional Blind Spots in Vision-Language-Action Models
lead_dispositions.evidence: Paper tests distractor placements in simulated LIBERO/VLA-Arena, not changes in robot location. F1 is 0.678 across five policies; targeted LoRA cuts failure 40–85%.

proposed_fields.one_line: Grid-based testing locates distractor placements that raise VLA failure: average F1 0.678 across five policies on simulated LIBERO/VLA-Arena. Targeted LoRA fine-tuning cuts failure rates 40-85%.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: The mechanism is described loosely. A 'positional blind spot' is a workspace region where moving a task-irrelevant distractor there sharply raises failure risk, with everything else held fixed. It is not simply a region 'where VLAs fail'. The setting (five VLAs on the LIBERO and VLA-Arena sim benchmarks) is also missing. The numbers themselves are correct.

lead_dispositions.name: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (Second Edition)
lead_dispositions.evidence: Authors’ page provides PDF, errata, code and slides. Exercise solutions are exchanged for a reader’s contributed solutions rather than freely published as a complete public set.

proposed_fields.one_line: Sutton and Barto's RL textbook (2nd ed., MIT Press 2018); the authors' page hosts the full PDF, errata, code and teaching slides, and trades official exercise solutions for your own. General RL background.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Small overclaim: the authors' page does not host exercise solutions. It offers an exchange where you send in your own solutions for a chapter and get the official ones back, and it marks this as currently incomplete. Everything else on the page matches: full PDF, errata, code, slides, MIT Press 2018.

lead_dispositions.name: Brax
lead_dispositions.evidence: README states that only brax/training remains maintained since version 0.13.0. It directs environment use to MuJoCo Playground and physics to MJX/MuJoCo Warp.

proposed_fields.one_line: Differentiable JAX physics engine with PPO, SAC, ARS, ES and APG trainers on accelerators; since 0.13.0 only brax/training is maintained, with environments via MuJoCo Playground and physics via MJX or MuJoCo Warp.

lead_dispositions.problem_in_lead: Typo: the one_line ends with a double period ('MJX..'). It also merges two separate pieces of README guidance: MuJoCo Playground replaces brax/envs, while MJX or MuJoCo Warp replaces Brax for physics. The content is otherwise accurate.
